title: DSA core: graphs, BFS/DFS and topological sort
seriesDescription: Language-independent interview topics (concepts, SQL, design, AI engineering): no Java and no Python code or library names.
description: Language-independent graph reasoning: BFS versus Dijkstra, multi-source BFS, tree conditions, cycle detection, Kahn's algorithm and counting problems.
source: LeetCode problem set and discuss; NeetCode roadmap; Cracking the Coding Interview; CLRS (graph algorithms)

questions.prompt: Match each problem with the standard graph technique.

left.text: Shortest path in an unweighted graph
Course schedule (can all courses be finished)

right.text: DFS or BFS flood fill counting components
BFS, since the first time a node is reached is the shortest
Kahn's algorithm or DFS cycle detection
DFS or BFS with a map from old node to copy

questions.explanation: Name the technique and the data structure it needs: flood fill needs a visited marker, BFS a queue, topological sort in-degrees or colours.

questions.prompt: In the grid [[2,1,1],[1,1,0],[0,1,1]], 2 is a rotten orange, 1 is fresh, 0 is empty. Each minute, rot spreads to the 4 neighbours of every rotten orange. How many minutes until no fresh orange remains?
questions.explanation: Minute 1 rots (0,1) and (1,0); minute 2 rots (0,2) and (1,1); minute 3 rots (2,1); minute 4 rots (2,2). That is the BFS depth from the single source.

questions.prompt: Why enqueue every rotten orange at the start (distance 0) instead of running a separate BFS from each?

options.text: One BFS gives every cell its nearest-source distance.
options.why: Correct: all sources expand in lockstep, so each cell is first reached from its closest source.

options.text: It lets you swap the queue for a recursive DFS and keep the levels.
options.why: DFS does not preserve distance order; the queue is what gives levels.

options.text: It is required to detect cycles in the grid before spreading.
options.why: Cycle detection plays no part in this problem.

options.text: It means you no longer need any visited marker anywhere in the grid.
options.why: You still need to mark cells so they are not queued twice.

questions.explanation: The trick generalises: walls and gates, distance to nearest zero, 01 matrix. Add a virtual super-source in your head.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Graph DFS needs a visited set to terminate, whereas a tree DFS usually does not.
questions.reason: A graph can contain cycles, so you can return to a node you already explored.

whys.a: Correct: without marking, a cycle makes the traversal loop forever; a tree has no cycles.
whys.b: R is the direct reason, so "does not explain" is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so this is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so this is wrong.

questions.explanation: In a tree you can only go to children, so you never revisit; in a graph you must remember what you have seen.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Plain BFS finds the cheapest path in a graph whose edges have different positive weights.
questions.reason: BFS visits nodes in increasing order of the number of edges from the source.

whys.a: A is false, so no explanation can hold.
whys.b: A is false, so both-true options cannot be right.
whys.c: R is true, so option c is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: BFS minimises the number of edges, not total weight, so use Dijkstra (priority queue) for weighted edges.

questions.explanation: Use 0-1 BFS with a double-ended queue when weights are only 0 or 1, and Dijkstra for general non-negative weights.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Both Kahn's algorithm and DFS with three colours can detect a cycle in a directed graph.
questions.reason: Kahn's algorithm reports a cycle when it outputs fewer nodes than the graph has.

whys.a: R only describes one of the two methods and does not explain why DFS also works.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but R explains only Kahn's test, not the statement about both methods.
whys.c: A is true, so this is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so this is wrong.

questions.explanation: DFS reports a cycle when it meets a node that is still on the current path (a back edge).

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Kahn's algorithm processes fewer than n nodes exactly when the directed graph has a cycle.
questions.reason: On a cycle, every node of the cycle starts with in-degree zero.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, so no both-true option applies.
whys.c: Correct: A is true, but R is false: every node on a cycle has an incoming edge from the cycle, so none of them ever reaches in-degree zero.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Cycle nodes block each other: each waits for another cycle node to be processed first.

questions.prompt: Edges: 0->1, 1->2, 2->1, 2->3 (4 nodes). Kahn's algorithm starts with the nodes of in-degree 0. How many nodes does it leave unprocessed when it finishes?
questions.explanation: Only node 0 has in-degree 0. Removing it lowers node 1 from 2 to 1, which is not zero, so the algorithm stops with nodes 1, 2 and 3 unprocessed. Nodes 1 and 2 form the cycle; node 3 is stuck behind it.

questions.prompt: A DAG has edges 0->1, 0->2, 1->3, 2->3. How many different valid topological orders does it have?
questions.explanation: Node 0 must come first and 3 last; nodes 1 and 2 can appear in either order: 0,1,2,3 and 0,2,1,3.

questions.prompt: In clone graph, why keep a map from each original node to its copy?

options.text: It lets you sort the neighbours before copying.
options.why: The map has nothing to do with ordering.

options.text: It reduces memory because copies share the originals' neighbour lists.
options.why: Copies must have their own neighbour lists, or it is not a deep copy.

options.text: It is only needed for directed graphs.
options.why: Undirected graphs have cycles on every edge, so they need the map even more.

options.text: It stops cycles and shared neighbours being copied twice.
options.why: Correct: the map both prevents infinite recursion on cycles and reuses a copy for a node reached by two routes.

questions.explanation: Register the copy before recursing into the neighbours; that ordering is what breaks the cycle.

questions.prompt: Which statements about BFS on an unweighted graph are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The first time BFS reaches a node is along a shortest path in number of edges.
options.why: Correct: nodes are reached in non-decreasing order of distance.

options.text: With an adjacency list it runs in O(V + E).
options.why: Correct: each vertex is queued once and each edge examined once or twice.

options.text: The queue can hold at most the nodes of two adjacent levels at once.
options.why: Correct: the queue contains nodes of level d and level d+1 only.

options.text: It must use recursion, otherwise the visited set does not work.
options.why: False: BFS is iterative with a queue; recursion plays no part.

questions.explanation: These three facts are why BFS is the default for fewest-steps questions.

questions.prompt: Word ladder: change one letter per step, every intermediate word must be in the list [hot, dot, dog, lot, log, cog]. How many words are in the shortest sequence from "hit" to "cog", counting both ends?
questions.explanation: hit -> hot -> dot -> dog -> cog (or via lot and log) has 5 words. Treat every word as a node and every one-letter change as an edge, then run BFS.

questions.prompt: An undirected graph has n nodes. Which condition sets, taken on their own, prove it is a tree? Select all that apply.

options.text: It is connected and has exactly n - 1 edges.
options.why: Correct: a connected graph needs at least n - 1 edges, and exactly n - 1 leaves no room for a cycle.

options.text: It has no cycle and has exactly n - 1 edges.
options.why: Correct: an acyclic graph with n - 1 edges must be connected.

options.text: It is connected and has exactly n edges.
options.why: False: n edges on n connected nodes means exactly one cycle.

options.text: It has no cycle and every node has an edge.
options.why: False: two separate acyclic components still satisfy this, so it need not be connected.

questions.explanation: Any two of "connected", "acyclic", "n - 1 edges" imply the third.

questions.prompt: What must a DFS cycle check handle on an undirected graph that the directed version does not?

options.text: It must run twice, once on the graph and once on its reverse.
options.why: Reversing an undirected graph changes nothing, so a second run adds nothing.

options.text: It must ignore the edge back to the node it just came from.
options.why: Correct: every undirected edge appears in both directions, so the parent would otherwise look like a cycle.

options.text: It must use three colours instead of a plain visited set.
options.why: Three colours are for directed graphs; undirected graphs need only the parent check.

options.text: It must sort every adjacency list before it starts the search.
options.why: Sorting has no effect on whether a cycle exists.

questions.explanation: Track the parent in the recursion. With union-find, an edge whose endpoints are already connected closes a cycle.

questions.text: BFS uses a {1} (first in, first out) and runs in O(V + E) on an adjacency {2}; mark a node visited when you {3} it so it is never queued twice.
questions.explanation: An adjacency matrix would make BFS O(V^2). Marking at enqueue time keeps the queue free of duplicates.

questions.prompt: Write pseudocode for bfsDistance(adj, start, goal), which returns the fewest edges from start to goal in an unweighted graph given as an adjacency list, or -1 if goal is unreachable.

checks.label: uses a queue seeded with the start node
keeps a visited set or distance table
loops until the queue is empty
visits each neighbour of the removed node
returns the distance when the goal is reached and -1 otherwise

questions.explanation: The first time BFS reaches the goal is along a shortest path, so you can return immediately. The distance table doubles as the visited set.
